description: Cross-model tests of ten writing-style prompts designed to produce prose far from common LLM writing defaults.

kind.control: baseline or bare label, to measure what a label bundles
kind.posture: one axis moved, everything else held; composable
kind.composite: a named point in the space, assembled from posture clauses
kind.costume: a whole format worn over the content; not decomposable

fidelity.rhetorical: claims preserved, emphasis and order may change
fidelity.interpretive: may add a stated perspective; must not contradict a source fact

_conventions.coordinates: design intent, not measurement. -1 / 0 / +1 on each axis. Replace with measured values once you score outputs.

density.+1: Pack related propositions into as few sentences as clarity allows, using embedding and compact noun phrases.
density.-1: Give each proposition its own sentence. Never fuse two ideas into one clause.

shared_ground.+1: Assume the reader already knows the actors, setting and background. Delete recoverable setup and explanation.
shared_ground.-1: Assume the reader has no background at all. Make every actor, referent and relationship explicit, using only what the text supplies.

omission.+1: Remove one or two inferences a competent reader can safely reconstruct, and state nothing twice.
omission.-1: State every intermediate step. Leave nothing for the reader to infer.

link_explicitness.+1: State every causal, contrastive, temporal and conditional relationship with an explicit connective.
link_explicitness.-1: Drop connectives and let sentence order carry the relationships, but only where they stay unambiguous.

writer_presence.+1: Make the writer visible and situated: who is speaking, what they saw, what they are answerable for.
writer_presence.-1: Keep the writer entirely off the surface. No first person and no visible narrator.

agency.+1: Foreground the responsible actor in every clause where the text names or implies one.
agency.-1: Foreground the process rather than the actor. Do not fall back on passive voice; restructure instead.

stance_marking.+1: Make the status of each claim visible: what is observed, what is inferred, what is asserted. Match the text's certainty exactly.
stance_marking.-1: State claims without marking how they are known. Remove epistemic framing while leaving the underlying certainty unchanged.

social_force.+1: Turn every requested action into a direct instruction with an owner.
social_force.-1: Turn every requested action into an option or an invitation, without weakening how certain the underlying claims are.

architecture.+1: Build hierarchical sentences. Attach every condition, exception and qualification precisely to what it modifies.
architecture.-1: One clause per sentence. No subordination.

sequence.+1: Put the conclusion in the first sentence. Order what follows by how much it would move a sceptical reader.
sequence.-1: Place the central conclusion last. Order the material so each step makes the next feel unavoidable.

concreteness.+1: Use the most specific noun and verb the text supports: a named role, a number, a moment. Keep an abstraction only where the text supplies no instance.
concreteness.-1: State the general case that each specific detail is an instance of, without losing the detail's content.

rhythm.+1: Vary sentence length sharply. Set at least one sentence under five words against a developed one.
rhythm.-1: Keep every sentence within a narrow length band.

_conventions.hold_constant_clause: Change nothing else. Everything the instruction does not name — vocabulary, length, sentence complexity, writer visibility, certainty, connectives, amount of information — stays as close to the text above as you can manage.

contracts.semantic: Add no fact, example, cause, motive, judgement or conclusion that is not in the text above. Keep every claim, qualification, contrast, negation and requested action. Do not make the text more or less certain, or more or less forceful, than it already is. Write in the source language, using that language's own devices rather than English ones. Output only the rewrite.
contracts.rhetorical: Add no fact, example, cause or conclusion that is not in the text above. You may reorder, re-emphasise, and change what is left implicit. Every claim and qualification must stay recoverable. Write in the source language, using that language's own devices rather than English ones. Output only the rewrite.
contracts.interpretive: Every claim you take from the text above must stay accurate, and you must never contradict a source fact. You may add perspective or inference, but keep it clearly the writer's own. Write in the source language. Output only the rewrite.

_conventions.compose: new prompt = one clause per non-zero axis, + hold_constant_clause if atomic, + the matching contract

Basically what happens is we pull the vendor files at 2am, and then there's a validation step, and the validation step is where most of the time goes, I think, because it's checking every row against the reference tables and those are in the same database. Also the retries. If a vendor file is late we retry the whole batch, not just that vendor, which means one late vendor can push everything past the 6am SLA. We missed the SLA eleven times last quarter. Priya's team suggested moving validation to a separate read replica, which would help, but it doesn't fix the retry problem. There was also a suggestion to just increase the window to 8am but the trading desk needs the data by 7. I think the retry thing is actually the bigger issue but I might be wrong about that. We should probably look at both. Someone needs to own this, right now it's kind of split between two teams and nothing moves.

The onboarding data is the most suggestive of the three, though our tracking was broken for nine days in the middle of the month, so that evidence has a gap.

The proposed test: roll onboarding out to the enterprise tier. If churn moves the same way there, we treat onboarding as the cause. If it doesn't, we've spent a quarter with nothing to show.

**Two things worth flagging in the original**

- It says "two of the three could explain it," then lists three plausible causes. Which one are you ruling out, and on what basis? Cutting the free tier is the obvious suspect — it changes *who* is in the denominator, not just how they behave.
- The enterprise test won't "settle it" as cleanly as stated. Enterprise users differ from the original cohort, so a matching result is suggestive rather than conclusive, and the free-tier change doesn't apply there at all. Conversely, a null result isn't a wasted quarter — it's meaningful evidence against onboarding, which redirects attention to the other two causes. Consider also whether a cheaper test exists: a holdout within the current tier, or a look at cohorts that were already past onboarding when the free tier was cut.

# Formal Rewrite

Following the launch of the redesigned onboarding flow, churn declined by four percentage points. However, two additional changes were implemented during the same period: the elimination of the free tier and the initiation of outbound sales contact with all trial registrants. Any of these three interventions could plausibly account for the observed improvement.

The evidence supporting the onboarding hypothesis appears strongest, though this conclusion must be qualified by a nine-day interruption in data collection during the middle of the measurement window.

We propose to extend the new onboarding flow to the enterprise tier. Should churn respond comparably in that segment, the matter would be resolved. Should it fail to do so, we will have expended a full quarter without a definitive finding.

---

## Two notes on the reasoning, offered separately from the rewrite

**On the proposed test.** A confirming result in the enterprise tier would strengthen the onboarding hypothesis but would not, strictly speaking, settle the question. Enterprise customers differ from self-serve customers in contract structure, switching costs, and buying process, so a positive result there may not isolate the same mechanism. Conversely, a null result would be similarly ambiguous — it could indicate that onboarding was never the driver, or simply that the intervention does not transfer to a segment with different churn dynamics. You may wish to soften "settles it" to something like "would provide substantial corroboration."

**On the tracking gap.** The nine-day interruption may bear more weight than the original framing suggests. If the free-tier change or the outbound calling program began during or near that window, the relative strength of the onboarding evidence could rest partly on missing data rather than on the data itself. It would be worth confirming the timing of all three changes against the gap before characterizing one hypothesis as strongest.

## GLOSS OF THE FIRST HAND

*written not long after, in the operations tradition*

> "Two of the three could explain it."

Note first the discipline of this sentence, which is greater than it appears. The writer does not say all three. Three things happened in one month, and the writer has already ruled one of them out on grounds not recorded here — a subtraction performed before the page begins. That the grounds go unstated is a defect of the record, not of the reasoning; a practitioner who has narrowed three candidates to two has done most of the work that can be done from the armchair. My own view is that the omission tells us the exclusion was obvious to everyone in the room at the time, which is how the most important premises usually go missing.

> "The onboarding data looks strongest."

Here the writer is honest in a way that costs something. *Looks* is doing real work: it is a report of an impression, not a finding, and it sits immediately beside the admission that tracking broke for nine days in the middle. The writer volunteers the weakness of the very evidence being leaned on. I read this as the mark of someone who intends to be corrected.

> "If we roll onboarding out to the enterprise tier and churn moves the same way, that settles it."

This is the sound instinct. You cannot separate three simultaneous events by staring at them; you can only move one of them and watch. The enterprise rollout does exactly this — it takes the suspected cause and applies it somewhere the other two events are not sitting on top of it. And observe that the writer has priced the downside in advance: *we have spent a quarter.* A quarter is the cheapest currency in which such a question has ever been settled. I would have shipped it the same week.

## GLOSS OF THE SECOND HAND

*a later era, after the causal turn*

> "If it does not, we have spent a quarter."

My predecessor admires this line as accounting. I read it as a confession, and the most revealing sentence on the page. Consider the structure: one branch of the experiment yields *that settles it*, and the other yields only a bill. A test whose failure produces an expense rather than a conclusion is not a test; it is a wager with a stated stake and an unstated payout. Had the writer been able to say what a null result would mean, the writer would have said it here. Nothing in the text supplies that half.

> "That settles it."

Settles *what*, and among whom? The four-point drop was observed in a population; the rollout is proposed for the enterprise tier, which is by construction a different one. Whatever the writer thinks a confirmation there would license, my own judgment is that the strongest such result establishes that onboarding does something for enterprise customers — a fact of real value, and not the fact under dispute. The word *settles* is where the writer's confidence exceeds the writer's design.

> "Our tracking broke for nine days in the middle."

My predecessor calls this honesty and moves on. I call it the load-bearing sentence. The writer's own ranking places the onboarding data first, and the writer's own record places a nine-day hole inside it. So the strongest evidence and the largest gap are the same object. I do not say the four points are unreal — the drop is given, and I take it as given. I say only that the interval where the mechanism would have been visible is precisely the interval that was not recorded, and that a rollout designed to confirm an impression will tend to confirm it.

> "Two of the three could explain it."

The earlier hand treats this narrowing as work completed. I treat it as work concealed. Two live explanations remain on the page, unnamed and unranked against each other, and the proposed quarter tests only one. Whatever comes back, the other will still be standing.

**First gloss — a near hand, still inside the same quarter.**

> *"we retry the whole batch, not just that vendor"*

Here is the whole matter, and the author knows it, which is why he says plainly that the retry is the bigger issue. Read the two proposals against each other. The read replica attacks the *duration* of a good run: validation stops contending with the reference tables in the same database, and the run gets shorter. Useful. But the eleven misses were not caused by a run being uniformly long; they were caused by a run being *restarted*. A faster validation that is performed twice is not obviously better than a slow validation performed once. The author's hedge — *I think* — is honest bookkeeping about where the seconds go, not doubt about which defect is structural. My gloss, and it is mine: the retry granularity is a design choice, and a design choice can be changed without buying anything. The batch is treated as indivisible when the only genuinely indivisible thing is a vendor's own file. Fix the unit of retry first; then measure validation, and let the replica be justified on numbers rather than on plausibility. As for the 8am proposal, it deserves the short answer it got. It does not shorten anything. It relabels.

### ADEYEMI, *Marginalia*, written three years after

> "*the review checklist does not mention worker counts*"

Here is the whole matter, and the report almost buries it in the final clause. A change that halved the worker pool passed through review because the instrument of review had no line on which such a change could be recorded. One person signed it. I do not say the reviewer was careless — the text does not say so, and I will not invent it — I say only that the reviewer was handed a document that did not ask the relevant question, and answered the questions it did ask.

Everything downstream follows from that omission. The eight minutes before the alert was seen, the twenty-nine minutes of wrong hypothesis, the thirteen minutes from escalation to revert, the twenty-seven minutes of drain: seventy-seven minutes end to end, and none of it would have been spent had the previous evening's review contained one additional line. My own view, which the text does not supply: an incident whose cause was deployed the night before and reverted in thirteen minutes once seen is not an operational failure at all. It is a change-management failure wearing operational clothing. Amend the checklist. Require a second reviewer for anything touching capacity. The queue drained on its own once the cause was removed, which tells us the running system was sound; the defect entered through the door marked *approved*.

### KESTREL, *Second Gloss*, from a later era, when configuration is generated and deploys are hourly

> "*was read as the weekly reconciliation job, which had produced a similar spike a month earlier*"

Adeyemi reads the last clause and stops. I read this one, and find it the only sentence in the record with anything to teach.

Consider what was available at 09:22. A queue backing up; a memory of a month-old spike that looked like this. The reading was not foolish. It was the best-supported story in the room, and it was wrong, and being wrong it held for twenty-nine minutes — during which a customer called at 09:40, eleven minutes before escalation. The record does not tell us whether that call was what broke the hypothesis, and I will not pretend it does. But note the shape: the system's own alarm produced a plausible false explanation, and a person outside the system produced the doubt. That is worth more than any checklist line.

To Adeyemi's remedy I say: you propose to add *worker counts* to a document, and by doing so you will catch this change and no other. The next change will not be a worker count. The checklist is a list of the ways we have already been surprised; its omissions are not accidents to be corrected one by one, they are the definition of the thing. In my era we abandoned the single reviewer not because reviewers are weak but because review scales worse than change does — and I concede that the text records only one reviewer here, not that one was insufficient by policy.

> "*About 4,000 payments delayed; none lost*"

This is the load-bearing fact, and both the report and Adeyemi treat it as a consolation. It is not consolation, it is evidence. Four thousand payments sat in a queue for up to seventy-seven minutes and every one of them survived a halved worker pool, a wrong diagnosis, and a revert. Durability held under exactly the conditions it exists for. What did not hold was the inference — the leap from *this looks like last month* to *this is last month*.

So: build for the twenty-nine minutes, not for the missing line. Make the second hypothesis cheap to test. Put the previous evening's deploys in front of the on-call engineer's face at 09:22, unasked. Adeyemi would have prevented this incident. I would prefer to shorten the next one, whose cause is not yet on anybody's list.

I concur in the decision and write separately only to place my reservations on the record.

1. I accept the finding. After four terms I agree that the hard part of this work is choosing what to leave out, and that it is harder than explaining well. My reservations concern the use to which the finding may later be put, not its correctness.

2. What has changed, on the record, is the ranking of two difficulties. It does not follow that the first has ceased to be difficult. This becomes a problem if the decision is afterwards cited as authority for treating explaining well as the easy part, and for withdrawing effort from it accordingly.

3. Each added topic was added because a student asked. That was a reason, and it was accepted at the time, once a year, in each instance. This becomes a problem if the additions are henceforth considered only in the aggregate, as course length, and removed on that footing; the decision determines that something must be left out but says nothing about what is owed to the student who asked.

4. The record shows two developments advancing together across the years: the course gets longer, and the students get more anxious. It establishes their coincidence. This becomes a problem if the decision is read as authority for the further proposition that shortening the course will relieve the anxiety.

5. I accept that the session in which the projector failed was the best session of last term, and that it consisted of forty minutes and a whiteboard. I note that the conditions were not chosen. This becomes a problem if it is assumed that adopting the same constraints deliberately will produce the same session, since the record contains one such occasion in four terms, and the occasion arose by failure.

6. The record states that bravery is what has so far been lacking. It does not establish that bravery is all that is lacking. This becomes a problem if the session is planned on purpose, does not go as the unplanned one did, and the outcome is attributed to insufficient courage.

7. The additions occurred every year, on the same occasion: a student asked. Whatever practice of omission follows from this decision will meet that occasion again. This becomes a problem if the decision is left standing as a resolution taken once, since it does not, of itself, bind next year.

8. Subject to the foregoing, I join the decision.

**Gloss I. Marginal note in a training-college handbook, mid-century**

*"After four terms I think it is choosing what to leave out."*

Four terms is not long, and the writer does not pretend otherwise; he offers the sentence as a revision, not a law. Still, I would not dismiss it for youth. The revision has the right shape. Explanation is the part of the work that flatters us, because it can be practised alone and admired in the moment. Selection cannot be admired at all — no one applauds the topic you did not teach — and so it is the part that goes untrained.

Notice the mechanism he reports, which is more damning than the confession that follows it. *"Every year I add a topic because a student asked."* Each addition is individually kind. He does not say the additions are wrong; he says the course gets longer and the students get more anxious, and he sets those two facts side by side without joining them. I will join them, on my own authority: a course that answers every question asked of it teaches, by its shape, that the subject is unfinishable. The anxiety is not a by-product of the length. It is the length, understood by the students correctly.

From which the duty follows plainly. He has already found his best hour and named its conditions — forty minutes, a whiteboard, and nothing else available. He calls his failure to plan for it a want of bravery. I would call it the ordinary reluctance to give up an alibi. Build the constrained session on purpose; let the projector fail by appointment.

**Gloss II. Seminar remarks, some decades later**

*"I have not been brave enough to plan for that on purpose."*

My predecessor reads this as a man withholding an act of courage from himself, and then hands him the act. I think the sentence is doing something else, and that taking it as a resolution ruins it.

Consider what the writer actually claims about that session. He says it was the best he ran *last term*, and he names its circumstances: the projector failed, and he had forty minutes and a whiteboard. He does not claim the whiteboard was the cause. That inference is ours, and I think it is at least half wrong. Something else was in the room: a man improvising in real time, deciding in front of witnesses what mattered enough to write down by hand. Scarcity of equipment produced an abundance of presence. Schedule the scarcity and you get the whiteboard back without the emergency — a lesson-plan with fewer slides and the same held breath. That is why the bravery is not simply available on request. What he would have to plan for is not a format but a state, and states do not take instructions.

I differ with the earlier reading on the additions, too. *"Every year I add a topic because a student asked"* — my predecessor hears softness. I hear a record. Every one of those topics is evidence of a live question in a real room, and a teacher who prunes on principle will cut some of them wrongly and never learn which. The writer's own diagnosis is that the hard part is choosing what to leave out; I would only add, and this is mine and not his, that the choosing is not the same act as the cutting. He is being asked to leave things out of forty minutes. Nobody said he had to leave them out of the subject.
